murray1946.title: Assessment of OSS Personnel
murray1946.author: Henry A. Murray and Donald W. MacKinnon
murray1946.quote: Construction Test. The candidate was shown a glorified tinker-toy with which he was instructed to build a 5-foot cube with 7-foot diagonals in ten minutes with the aid of 2 helpers whom he was to direct. The "helpers" were members of the junior staff who soon turned the situation into a test of the candidate's frustration-tolerance by becoming increasingly lazy, recalcitrant, and insulting. No candidate ever completed this task, and there were those who became either markedly upset or enraged by the humiliations they suffered. [...] Since there were, in all, 35 procedures, and since each procedure provided an opportunity to rate 1 to 4 variables, there were anywhere from 2 to 10 scores for every candidate on each of the 10 variables by the end of the three and a half days of assessment. [...] About 5,500 men and women went through the Assessment Centers in this country.
murray1946.note: Scan of the printed article opened at archive.org (item 'assesment-of-oss-personel'; the _djvu.txt OCR derivative of the same scan was read end to end). lenzenweger2015.title: Factors Underlying the Psychological and Behavioral Characteristics of Office of Strategic Services Candidates: The Assessment of Men Data Revisited
lenzenweger2015.author: Mark F. Lenzenweger
lenzenweger2015.quote: The challenge set for the OSS assessment team, which set up initial operations at the Willard Estate in Fairfax, VA, just outside of Washington, DC, at what was called Station S (for Schools and Training), was to define the criteria that would be central to the selection of OSS personnel. [...] The particularly difficult aspect of this challenge was that the fundamental nature of the ultimate "to be predicted" criterion (i.e., the "successful" OSS officer) was not known at the time the assessment enterprise was undertaken, nor could it have been known with certainty in advance (OSS Assessment Staff, 1948). In short, the OSS assessment staff did not know precisely what they were asked to predict in developing selection criteria for candidates. [...] The job of the "stooges" in this construction task was to be as maximally frustrating and difficult as they could be in relation to the candidate who was actually trying to build the small structure. [...] There were more than 50 professional staff at Station S, the main assessment center (there were several others), and more than 5,000 candidates were assessed there in a period of about 20 months across all OSS assessment sites (Handler, 2001). [...] it is reported that all records pertaining to the candidate evaluations conducted at Station S were ordered destroyed at the end of the war (Handler, 2001). Thus, this matrix is perhaps the only multivariate vestige of the herculean effort embodied in this important chapter of psychological assessment, an effort that gave birth to the modern assessment center approach that is in use today (Bhyham, 2002). [...] Once at Station S, the candidates were assessed on 85 to 90 assessments, which were reduced conceptually and used to inform the final ratings of the candidates on 10 core dimensions.
lenzenweger2015.note: Publisher PDF opened and read in full. Print issue year 2015; published online 18 Jul 2014. The reanalysis is of the single surviving correlation matrix (n=133) printed in Assessment of Men (1948), Appendix B, p. 510.

banks1995.title: The Office of Strategic Services Psychological Selection Program (MMAS thesis, U.S. Army Command and General Staff College)
banks1995.author: Louie M. Banks III
banks1995.venue: U.S. Army Command and General Staff College, Fort Leavenworth, Kansas; approved for public release
banks1995.quote: This concept reached its zenith when the candidates were given tasks to perform that they stood no chance of successfully completing, e.g., the Construction Test, and were measured instead on how they coped with the difficulty and stress involved. [...] This assessment was performed at no small cost and was the precursor to both the civilian personnel assessment center movement and to several Special Operations selection programs currently in existence. [...] In it, a candidate was given ten minutes to construct a five foot square box with an assortment of materials. He was assigned two "helpers," to perform the actual work. In fact, both helpers were stooges, one seemingly incompetent, and the other critical and aggressive. This task was never completed within the time limit [...] Several of the candidates actually physically attacked the helpers during the test, a measure of its intensity. [...] At total of 2,372 candidates were assessed there. Additionally, 3,071 candidates were assessed in Washington, D.C., mostly for administrative positions. [...] The candidates would stay at Station S for three and one-half days. [...] In mid 1943, following a war driven expansion and having recruited an ever [...] Over the next year and a half, more than five thousand prospective candidates were evaluated before acceptance into the OSS. [...] MacKinnon, one of the designers of the assessment program, and the director of Station S from June 1944 until V-J Day, in a 1980 review of the program stated that it was not very successful in predicting performance overseas and, "that the appraisal process as carried out left very much to be desired."

unverified: The names 'Kippy' and 'Buster' for the two staff helpers. These are widely repeated and are attributed to Assessment of Men (OSS Assessment Staff, Rinehart, 1948), but the 1948 book is lending-restricted on archive.org and Cloudflare-blocked on HathiTrust; no copy was opened. The names appear nowhere in the three sources that were opened, all of which call the helpers 'junior staff' or 'stooges'. They are therefore kept out of the prose and off the cards.

The exact month Station S accepted its first class. Banks 1995 dates the programme's origin to 'mid 1943'; Lenzenweger 2015 dates MacKinnon's British War Office Selection Board input to 1943 and gives a run of 'about 20 months'. No source opened here names a December 1943 opening date, so the seam tag says 1943 and no month is claimed.
Any dollar figure for the cost of the OSS assessment programme. Banks 1995 says only that it 'was performed at no small cost'. No currency amount is claimed in the prose.

The commonly repeated claim that the OSS method was lifted into AT&T's Management Progress Study in 1956 (Bray & Grant, Psychological Monographs 80(17), 1966). The APA and PsycNet records were unreachable and no copy of Bray & Grant was opened, so AT&T does not appear in the prose or on a card; the descent claim rests on Banks 1995 and Lenzenweger 2015, which both state it in general terms.

Whether the OSS staff themselves published a self-assessment of validity failure in Assessment of Men (1948). The validity limits stated in the prose come from Lenzenweger 2015, not from the 1948 book, which was not opened.

Whether candidates were being run through Station S in 1943, the year on the box tag. No opened source dates the first class: Banks 1995 puts the programme's origin at 'mid 1943' and Lenzenweger 2015 says professional assistance 'began in earnest in 1943', so the tag carries the founding year of the programme at that location and no month.

Any claim that the programme's predictive validity was never established. Murray 1946 reports a partial follow-up (of the first 300 cases, 6 in 100 unsatisfactory overseas) and Banks 1995 reports Wiggins's (1973) estimate that Station S raised correct selection decisions from 63% to 77% over chance, and that intelligence was a useful predictor of operational success. The prose therefore claims only what Lenzenweger 2015 states: the criterion itself was never defined.
